rows.operator: John Cayley and Daniel C. Howe, the project's artists, on the project's own site
rows.kind: in its own words, 'a collection of distributed, performative, quasi-autonomous poetic 'readers' — active, procedural entities with distinct reading behaviors and strategies'; its artist statement calls it 'an essay in digital language art'
rows.question: generative transformation: what an authored software reader writes as it reads a text, and how the source of each phrase it recomposes is kept
rows.unit: a reader (a coded reading behavior) deployed on a text, and the text it generates as it reads; How It Is in Common Tongues (2012) is a separately identified work, an artists' book recorded inside this row
rows.record_object: software readers (Simple, Perigram, Spawning, Mesostic, Grammatical) released onto found texts, reconfigured appropriated sources and the collaborators' own compositions; the texts those readers generate; How It Is in Common Tongues, a recomposition of Samuel Beckett's How It Is from phrases found by a search engine

record.in_layer: the readers read the texts they are released onto and draw word and phrase frequencies 'culled from the largest corpus of human language that has ever existed', made visible by web indexing; How It Is in Common Tongues quotes phrases from 'a portion of the commons of language that happens to have been indexed'; the saved sources name no model training
record.name: the readers' outputs are published as the project's work under Cayley and Howe; in How It Is in Common Tongues each found phrase is cited by URL, date and occurrence count, and the saved page states no author names for the phrases, which it says were 'composed by writers or writing machines other than Beckett'
record.readback: the project states it displays 'the primary source of a text generator's inputs' within that source's typographic environment, so the reading path can be followed on the source text; How It Is in Common Tongues gives for each phrase the shortest URL the readers retrieved, the date found and the total occurrences on that date, in hexadecimal notes
record.makes: new text generated in the course of reading: perigram readers diverge and generate 'an alternative text', a mesostic reader capitalizes letters in place to spell out a phrase, a grammatical reader jumps ahead 'leaving strange lacuna in the text while still preserving aspects of its style'; How It Is in Common Tongues recomposes Beckett's novel in sequence from the longest common phrases found elsewhere

rows.method: coded reading behaviors derived from 'a necessarily partial, aesthetically implicated analysis of human reading', moving through a text's typographic neighborhood and testing 3-gram completions against natural-language frequency data; How It Is in Common Tongues by searching Beckett's text through a search engine phrase by phrase

self_description.quote: The Readers Project is a collection of distributed, performative, quasi-autonomous poetic 'readers' — active, procedural entities with distinct reading behaviors and strategies.

surfaces.quote: We release these readers onto inscribed surfaces that are explicitly or implicitly, visibly or invisibly, constituted by their texts.

material.quote: The readers address themselves to a wide range of material — from conventional found texts, through poetic reconfigurations of appropriated sources, to original compositions by the project's collaborators.

partial_analysis.quote: Since their behaviors are derived from a necessarily partial, aesthetically implicated analysis of human reading,

deployed.quote: Many readers are under development. At the time of writing, half a dozen readers have been regularly deployed on various texts.

rereading.quote: The texts that our readers produce as they read, we claim, are worth rereading, a quality that is often cited as a mark of the literary.

essay.quote: This project is an essay in digital language art.

readers_write.quote: Further, because the project’s readers move within and are thus composed by the words within which they move, they also, effectively, write.

live.quote: published as real-time streams of live-writing, available to anyone with internet access.

display_source.quote: The Readers Project is innovative, however, in having found a number of ways to display the primary source of a text generator’s inputs within this source’s typographically structured literary environment.

corpus_frequencies.quote: its use of current natural language information—especially concerning the relative frequencies of words and phrases considered by the readers—culled from the largest corpus of human language that has ever existed

artist_cayley.quote: John Cayley makes digital language art, particularly in the domain of poetry and poetics.

artist_howe.quote: Daniel C. Howe is an artist, writer, and critical technologist

citing.quote: Howe, Daniel C., and Cayley, John. Reading, Writing, Resisting: Literary Appropriation in the Readers Project.

reader_types.quote: Simple Reader Perigram Reader Spawning Reader Mesostic Reader Grammatical Reader

unconstrained.quote: The Unconstrained Perigram Reader is a variety of the Perigram Reader that is less constrained than its cousin.

perigram_alternative.quote: If it finds a completing word then its reading path may diverge, effectively also generating an alternative text.

mesostic.quote: When it finds a word that contains a required letter, the reader capitalizes the letter in place.

grammatical.quote: leaving strange lacuna in the text while still preserving aspects of its style.

hiiict_method.quote: How It Is in Common Tongues was composed by searching for the text of Samuel Beckett’s How It Is using a universally accessible search engine, attempting to find, in sequence, the longest common phrases from How It Is that were composed by writers or writing machines other than Beckett.

hiiict_commons.quote: These phrases are quoted from a portion of the commons of language that happens to have been indexed by a universally accessible engine.

hiiict_outcome.quote: How It Is in Common Tongues is an art work, and an aesthetic outcome of The Readers Project .

hiiict_counts.quote: The number following the date (or ‘id.’) is the total number of occurrences found for the phrase, as searched on that date and for the search engine we used.

hiiict_hex.quote: These note numbers are in hexadecimal.

hiiict_pdf.quote: The work is downloadable as a pdf .

hiiict_montfort.quote: It was noted by Nick Montfort as a Radical Book of 2012 .

self_description.quote: National Novel Generation Month - based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted on a whim .

goal.quote: Spend the month of November writing code that generates a novel of 50k+ words. This is in the spirit of National Novel Writing Month 's interesting definition of a novel as 50,000 words of fiction.

rule.quote: The only rule is that you share at least one novel and also your source code at the end.

code_license.quote: The source code does not have to be licensed in a particular way, so long as you share it. The code itself does not need to be on GitHub, either.

github.quote: We're just using this repo as a place to organize the community.

novel_defined.quote: The "novel" is defined however you want. It could be 50,000 repetitions of the word "meow". It could literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg.

copyright.quote: Please try to respect copyright. We're not going to police it, as ultimately it's on your head if you want to just copy/paste a Stephen King novel or whatever
